newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: EU citizens need to be told why euro good for them.
newsitem.headline: EU citizens need to be told why euro good for them.

text.p: The European Union must do a better job to explain to its citizens why they would benefit from joining a single currency, EU Commissioner for monetary affairs Yves-Thibault de Silguy said on Friday.

"The main problem today is the lack of information available to European citizens. Eighty to 90 percent of Europeans consider themselves badly informed about the euro (single currency)," Silguy said during a visit to Lisbon.

"We (EU) have to make an effort to explain why the euro is a good thing for the economy, for our competitiveness and for our consumers," he said after meeting Portuguese Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco.
"I am convinced that if we explain to people simply and correctly why the euro is a good thing, we will convince them," he added.
The euro will make the European economy more competitive with the rest of the world and end currency instability among member states, he said.
Polls indicate that the British have turned sharply against the European Union while the vast majority of Germans want a referendum on a single currency.

Silguy said the other priorities before the launch of the euro on January 1, 1999 were the continuing efforts by member states to control their public finances and for companies and banks to adapt to the euro.
"It is vital that banks and companies multiply their efforts to be ready because the first to be ready for the euro will gain the most," he said.
Silguy said that the Portuguese economy had made good progress towards convergence with other EU states.
"The Portuguese economy is converging with the rest of Europe," he said. "The results are quite encouraging."
Portugal has cut real interest rates, inflation and its budget deficit in recent years and economists say it has a fighting chance to join the euro from its launch.
The Socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres has said it is committed to joining the euro from the start.
Silguy declined to comment on Portugal's chances of joining the euro or to compare its performance with neighbouring Spain.
"All countries will be judged on the same criteria," he said. "We will appraise the sustainability of convergence -- not just the willingness of countries to converge their economies."
EU states must meet a set of tough entry conditions to join the euro, such as reducing their budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product and keeping a tight lid on inflation.
